q-161927.problem:

q-161927.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-2z,\,0,\,0⟩{|}_{z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨-2(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨{{2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20)\cdot (-2x)-0\cdot (-2y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14274664/assets/c181e209cca01a1d6e372caa7f7810a5fa4aa9f177595bd92f937a7cba8b8a75.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\,4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-162314.name: Question 2
q-162314.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=(2{t}^{3}-2t)\,i+(t+{t}^{2})\,j+(-t-{t}^{2})\,k$ for $t\in [-1,0).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=y\,i+x\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
q-162314.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=2{t}^{3}-2t,\,y=t+{t}^{2},\,z=-t-{t}^{2}.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =y\,i+x\,k \\  & =(t+{t}^{2})\,i+(2{t}^{3}-2t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+{t}^{2})\,j-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t-{t}^{2})\,k \\  & =(6{t}^{2}-2)\,i+(1+2t)\,j+(-1-2t)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((t+{t}^{2})\,i+(2{t}^{3}-2t)\,k)\cdot ((6{t}^{2}-2)\,i+(1+2t)\,j+(-1-2t)\,k) \\  & =(t+{t}^{2})\cdot (6{t}^{2}-2)+0\cdot (1+2t)+(2{t}^{3}-2t)\cdot (-1-2t) \\  & =2{t}^{4}+4{t}^{3}+2{t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(2{t}^{4}+4{t}^{3}+2{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[\frac{2{t}^{5}}{5}+{t}^{4}+\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =0-(-\frac{2}{5}+1-\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{15}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.

$$
z=g(x,y)=1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=4y\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨y,\,-x,\,1⟩{|}_{z=1+{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨y,\,-x,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨{{y}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{-x}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{1}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (2x)-(-x)\cdot (4y)+1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2xy+1)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}

q-162366.name: Question 4
q-162366.problem:
Use Stokes' theorem to evaluate 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,
$$

where $\text{curl}\,F=⟨-x{e}^{z},\,0,\,{e}^{z}⟩,$ and $C$ is the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=4.$ The curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above.
q-162366.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ and the plane $z=4.$ One such surface would be the plane $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=4.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4)=0 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into the expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-x{e}^{z},\,0,\,{e}^{z}⟩{|}_{z=4} \\  & =⟨{{-x{e}^{4}}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{{e}^{4}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-0\cdot (-x{e}^{4})-0\cdot 0+{e}^{4})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{4}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane.

Notice that the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ with radius $2$ centered at the origin. Therefore, using the change of variables to polar coordinates

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,\text{d}A=r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta ,
$$

 

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{e}^{4}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{4}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={e}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}r\,\text{d}r \\  & ={e}^{4}[\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}]}_{r=0}^{r=2} \\  & ={e}^{4}(2\pi -0)\cdot (2-0) \\  & =4\pi {e}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-162999.name: Question 5
q-162999.problem:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by the closed curve $C$ with positive orientation and parametrization $r(t)=({t}^{2}-t)\,i+({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\,j+({t}^{2}-t)\,k$ for $t\in [0,1).$
Given that $F(x,y,z)=2z\,i+3y\,k,$ evaluate the integral

$$
{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$
q-162999.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={t}^{2}-t,\,y={t}^{2}-{t}^{3},\,z={t}^{2}-t.
$$

So,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t)) & =2z\,i+3y\,k \\  & =(2{t}^{2}-2t)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3})\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-{t}^{3})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}-t)\,k \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(2t-3{t}^{2})\,j+(2t-1)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) & =((2{t}^{2}-2t)\,i+(3{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3})\,k)\cdot ((2t-1)\,i+(2t-3{t}^{2})\,j+(2t-1)\,k) \\  & =(2{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot (2t-1)+0\cdot (2t-3{t}^{2})+(3{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3})\cdot (2t-1) \\  & =(-3{t}^{3}+5{t}^{2}-2t)\cdot (2t-1) \\  & =2t-9{t}^{2}+13{t}^{3}-6{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot dr \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-9{t}^{2}+13{t}^{3}-6{t}^{4})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}+\frac{13}{4}{t}^{4}-\frac{6}{5}{t}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =1-3+\frac{13}{4}-\frac{6}{5} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let S be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary C with positive orientation. If a vector field F has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains S, then Stokes' theorem states that ∮CF⋅dr=∬ScurlF⋅dS.

Along the curve C, we have x=t2−t,y=t2−t3,z=t2−t.

So, F(r(t))=2zi+3yk=(2t2−2t)i+(3t2−3t3)k.

Computing r′(t), we get r′(t)=ddt(t2−t)i+ddt(t2−t3)j+ddt(t2−t)k=(2t−1)i+(2t−3t2)j+(2t−1)k.

Therefore, F(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((2t2−2t)i+(3t2−3t3)k)⋅((2t−1)i+(2t−3t2)j+(2t−1)k)=(2t2−2t)⋅(2t−1)+0⋅(2t−3t2)+(3t2−3t3)⋅(2t−1)=(−3t3+5t2−2t)⋅(2t−1)=2t−9t2+13t3−6t4.

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

∬ScurlF⋅dS=∮CF⋅dr=∫01F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫01(2t−9t2+13t3−6t4)dt=[t2−3t3+134t4−65t5]01=1−3+134−65=120
